items.title: When Does Workload Undermine Innovative Behavior? The Joint Moderating Roles of Empowering Leadership and Perceived Organizational Support
items.abstract: Drawing on the job demands–resources (JD–R) model, this study examines how workload relates to innovative behavior through emotional exhaustion. Prior research offers competing predictions regarding the consequences of workload, particularly from the JD–R model and the challenge–hindrance stressor perspective. Against this backdrop, we propose that workload is negatively related to innovative behavior through its positive association with emotional exhaustion. We further examine how two key job resources—empowering leadership and perceived organizational support (POS)—jointly shape this process. Using three‐wave, multisource data from 349 employees nested within 30 supervisors in a large Chinese firm, we find that workload is negatively associated with innovative behavior and that this relationship is partly explained by a significant negative indirect effect through emotional exhaustion. Moreover, empowering leadership attenuates the positive relationship between workload and emotional exhaustion, and this buffering effect is stronger when POS is high, as indicated by a significant three‐way interaction. These findings contribute to the JD–R literature by providing evidence consistent with the health‐impairment pathway and demonstrating how empowering leadership and POS jointly moderate the relationship between workload and emotional exhaustion.

items.title: When Reasoning looks like Hidden Understanding: How Chain-of-Thought Fosters Anthropomorphism, Perceptions of Epistemic Superiority, and Cognitive Deference
items.abstract: As AI-based products permeate society, specifically systems using generative models, a belief system is emerging about what these products are and what they can and cannot do. One common belief concerns the perception of the form of language as evidence of 'understanding' language. As these generative models reproduce linguistic patterns rather than understand meaning, interpreting these patterns as evidence of understanding is a misattribution. This misconception is extended by the notion that generative models can 'explain their reasoning.' Anecdotally, these misconceptions which mistake the form of language for its meaning are driving cognitive deference to AI systems in a way that displaces human agency. Such mistakes involve attributions of cognitive properties to the system, allowing them to be treated like intentional 'minds'. Importantly, perceived epistemic authority and superiority make that 'mind' worth deferring to. Anthropomorphism in tandem with epistemic authority and superiority, we argue, increases the risk that users generalise from narrow task performance to broader competencies, committing the "fallacy of composition". This paper explores misconceptions of Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning as sufficient transparent 'explanation'. We explore how anthropomorphism acts as a vehicle for cognitive deference of decision-making and perceptions of epistemic superiority in AI systems. Finally, we explore CoT's ramifications using medicine as an example. Taken together, we conclude that explainability operationalised through CoT is highly problematic and undercuts the very ethical principles it is intended to serve. items.title: When the Algorithm Sets the Pace: Digital Management, Worker Voice and Job Quality
items.abstract: Software that allocates tasks, sets the pace of work, monitors behaviour and rates performance has moved from delivery platforms into ordinary workplaces, yet comparative evidence on how widely it is used, who is shielded from it and what it does to job quality remains thin. This study reanalyses the published results of the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) OSH Pulse survey of about 27,250 workers in 29 countries (spring 2022) and sets them against the 2024 establishment survey (ESENER) and the 2025 OSH Pulse wave. A country-by-sector panel of the organisational model index shows that 63 percent of its variation lies between countries and 12 percent between sectors; sector rankings agree across countries (Kendall’s W = 0.28), with commerce, transport and food, ICT and finance, and administrative services highest. Countries with statutory agreement or co-determination rights over new technology do not show lower adoption (difference -0.11 index points; exact permutation p = 0.44). Published regressions link each additional digital management practice to 0.21 more psychosocial risks and 0.17 more health complaints; worker consultation is associated with reductions equal to 0.51 (95% interval 0.32 to 0.70) and 0.78 (0.50 to 1.06) of one practice. Raising consultation to all workers would offset 15 percent of the average psychosocial burden and 22 percent of the health burden, and a package of effective measures 53 and 74 percent. The findings are associations from self-reports, and the panel tests describe variation among cell means rather than sampling error. Purpose - This study measures the diffusion of digital worker management across European countries and sectors, asks whether worker voice institutions are associated with less adoption, and quantifies how far worker consultation offsets the job quality costs of digital management. Design/methodology/approach - The paper reanalyses published OSH Pulse 2022 results: a two-way variance decomposition and Tukey non-additivity test on a 29-country by 8-sector panel, Kendall’s W, exact permutation and bootstrap comparisons of voice regimes, and delta-method and Monte Carlo accounting built on published regression coefficients. Findings - Country differences dominate sector differences in adoption; sector ranks are stable; voice regimes are not associated with lower adoption; and consultation is associated with sizeable but partial offsets of psychosocial and health burdens. Research limitations/implications - The analysis uses published aggregates and coefficients, cross-sectional self-reports and a coarse regime classification, and cannot establish causal effects or test whether consultation moderates the effect of digital management. Practical implications - Employers and regulators should treat consultation on digital systems as one component of a package that includes information, awareness and transparency, and should extend algorithmic management safeguards beyond platform work. Social implications - Because most workers already experience some form of digital management, protection that applies only to platform workers will miss most of those affected. Originality/value - The paper brings comparative panel evidence, institutional comparison and transparent accounting together, and shows how the current regulatory and survey evidence on digital management fits.

items.title: Work Context and Work Style requirements across supply chain occupations: evidence from O*NET 30.3
items.abstract: Introduction Supply chain occupations differ in the discretion, coordination, pace, responsibility, and physical activity built into their work. We examined how these conditions correspond to the Work Style requirements associated with occupational performance and whether the resulting profiles distinguish task groups across conventional occupational families. Methods O*NET 30.3 supplied 57 Work Context elements, 21 Work Style Impact ratings, and 41 Work Activity Importance ratings. Principal component analysis (PCA) and permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) compared five families among 24 focal occupations. Elastic Net models were developed from 838 non-focal occupations to predict each Work Style for the 24 focal occupations. Multi-response partial least squares (PLS2) regression evaluated the joint context–style relation across all 862 occupations, and Ward clustering linked occupational profiles to Work Activities. Results Family membership accounted for 35.2% of Work Context variation and 64.5% of Work Style variation. Nine of 21 Work Styles had positive focal-sample R 2 ; self-confidence ( R 2 = 0.589) and stress tolerance ( R 2 = 0.478) were the strongest predictions, whereas empathy was poorly predicted ( R 2 = −2.632). Two clusters separated 19 occupations emphasizing information processing, decision making, and coordination from five emphasizing material handling, equipment operation, and physical work. Their Work Activity profiles differed ( R 2 = 0.314, p = 0.001). Discussion The occupational pattern links decision latitude, consequential responsibility, and coordination demands to particular behavioral requirements, while the task comparison identifies operational similarities that cross family boundaries. Together, the findings support job analysis that combines working conditions, performance-relevant Work Styles, and task content.

items.title: AI and Machine Learning in Strategic Decision-Making among Global IT Unicorns
items.abstract: Privately held technology firms valued at more than USD 1 billion (“unicorns”) make high-stakes strategic choices under extreme uncertainty: which markets to enter, when to pivot, how to price, and when to prepare for a public listing. Many have embedded artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) into these choices. This paper examines how the depth of AI/ML integration in strategic decision-making is related to decision speed, forecasting accuracy, decision quality, financial performance and strategic agility. Building on bounded rationality, dynamic-capabilities and data-driven-firm theory, we derive five hypotheses and test them on a purpose-built synthetic dataset of 200 global IT unicorns. In the simulated data, a one-standard-deviation increase in AI maturity is associated with 7.4 fewer days in the strategic decision cycle, 2.3 percentage points lower revenue-forecast error and 5.5 points higher decision quality (all p < 0.001). Associations with revenue growth, burn multiple and customer-acquisition payback are conditional on data governance: the interaction terms are statistically significant (p < 0.01), and the positive growth association is concentrated in firms with above-median governance. AI maturity also raises the odds of a successful strategic pivot (odds ratio 1.84) and of IPO readiness (1.79). Sector differences in AI maturity are large (F = 12.1, p < 0.001), whereas regional differences are only marginal (F = 2.1, p = 0.056). Results are stable to robust standard errors, to a rank-based correlation and to splitting the sample by region, but weaker with an alternative maturity proxy. Because the data are synthetic, every relationship reflects the assumptions of the generator. The contribution of the paper is therefore methodological: a transparent measurement framework, hypotheses and estimation strategy that can be re-run on real survey or proprietary data.

items.title: Beyond Personality: Purpose as a Decision Logic in Employment Trade-Offs among Generation Z
items.abstract: Purpose-driven work has lately become an increasingly important element of employment preferences, particularly among Generation Z. While prior research has primarily examined organisational purpose in relation to meaningful work, work attitudes, and individual characteristics, less is known about how purpose influences employment-related decision-making under trade-off conditions. This study addresses this gap by examining purpose orientation as a decision criterion shaping the acceptance of employment-related trade-offs.The analysis is based on a questionnaire survey conducted among 797 Hungarian higher education students, with a focused subsample of 309 respondents who identified organisational purpose as an important factor in job choice. Using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and logistic regression, the study investigates whether purpose orientation is associated with MBTI personality characteristics and how it relates to willingness to accept different types of trade-offs.The results indicate that personality-based characteristics provide limited explanatory value for purpose prioritisation in the present sample. By contrast, stronger purpose orientation is associated with a higher likelihood of accepting several employment-related trade-offs, including increased workload, reduced flexibility, lower bonuses, lower job stability, and lower salary. However, financial and security-related compromises remain relatively uncommon overall.These findings suggest that purpose operates as a bounded and context-dependent motivational factor within employment-related decision-making rather than as an unconditional driver of sacrifice. By framing purpose orientation as a criterion within multi-attribute employment decisions, the study contributes to the literature on meaningful work and motivation and provides practical implications for organisations seeking to attract and retain Generation Z employees.

items.title: Building World Models from Intrinsic Motivation
items.abstract: In the absence of extrinsic rewards or task supervision, human behavior is guided by intrinsic motivation---neural signals that drive curiosity, creativity, play, and other essential facets of intelligence. Intrinsic motivation plays an important developmental role in building robust world models that enable generalization and adaptation. Yet existing studies leave open how a broad range of intrinsic motivations interacts with world-model representation learning to support downstream control. This limits our understanding of which intrinsically collected experiences build reusable models. To address these gaps, we integrate 24 intrinsic objectives, including established methods and explicit variants spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency, into a common model-based reinforcement learning framework. We evaluate the world models they build through zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming environments, using three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. Curiosity-driven exploration with observation reconstruction yields the strongest aggregate family profile, although the best individual pairing depends on the experiment. In compositional vision-based tasks, intrinsic motivation derived from both episodic and lifelong novelty---providing a complementary memory to the world model's generic recurrent state---achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation. These findings motivate designing intrinsic motivation and representation learning jointly. Our results demonstrate world models as a powerful tool for measuring the quality of intrinsically motivated experience, and positions intrinsic motivation as a key ingredient for building world models autonomously.

items.title: Coevolution in generative AI content ecosystems: behaviour-risk feedback, governance chains and local stability boundaries
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence enables producers to reformulate risky content after moderation, creating feedback between behaviour and governance. We examine how joint weakening across governance stages and differences in response speeds affect risk, trust and local stability. We develop a dimensionless, uncalibrated governance--adaptation evolutionary game linking content producers, platform governance units and users. The model includes finite moderation capacity, provenance retention, trust memory and endogenous producer adaptation. In the tested factorial design, jointly weakening the governance channels increased risk and reduced trust and user-experienced quality; under a common favourable reference, joint deterioration exceeded the corresponding positive single-channel losses for all three outcomes. Along a prescribed composite continuation path, spectral analysis indicated that tenfold acceleration of either backlog or provenance dynamics shifted the estimated local-stability boundary toward stronger aggregate feedback, whereas tenfold acceleration of trust-memory dynamics shifted it toward weaker feedback. These results are conditional on the specified structures and operating states: matching the adaptation state alone did not ensure equivalent transient responses or local stability. The framework supports analysis of governance coordination and response timing; application to particular platforms requires empirical calibration and validation.

items.title: Counteracting threat bias: A longitudinal field experiment testing two interventions that expand managerial attention to opportunities under economic threat.
items.abstract: When economic threat is salient, managers focus on preventing losses and neglect the opportunities adaptation requires, a pattern termed threat bias. On the prevailing view, managerial attention is limited so that attention to threat comes at the expense of attention to opportunity: Restoring it means perceiving less threat or relaxing vigilance, and the remedy has been to divide the orientations across people or units. Drawing on regulatory focus theory, in which promotion and prevention are independent systems, I propose instead that threat bias reflects a situational construal: Salient threat makes prevention cues dominant, while promotion cues lie dormant, so their relation is not fixed. I test this with two brief construal-shaping interventions, one highlighting opportunities (opportunity) and one highlighting opportunities and threats (balanced), in a five-wave field experiment with 414 managers during the COVID-19 downturn, with voice rated by higher level managers blind to condition. Among unexposed managers, within-person increases in perceived threat were associated with lower promotion focus and opportunity-related voice, the threat-bias pattern. Both interventions weakened that association and raised promotion focus and opportunity-related voice relative to control, under sustained economic threat. The balanced intervention also increased prevention focus and threat-related voice; the opportunity intervention changed neither. Mean perceived threat was unchanged: The interventions altered how managers responded to threat, not how much threat they perceived. Intervention effects on voice grew over 3 months. Threat bias therefore reflects how managers construe the situation rather than an unavoidable trade-off between the orientations, and both can be raised in the same managers at once. items.title: De la autonomía emergente a la personalidad instrumental: reconstrucción dogmática de la responsabilidad en agentes inteligentes de frontera
items.abstract: Este artículo analiza las tensiones estructurales que la opacidad epistémica inherente a los modelos de frontera empleados en agentes inteligentes produce sobre las garantías constitucionales de motivación, trazabilidad y control jurisdiccional. La investigación parte de la constatación de que la autonomía emergente e imposibilidad técnica de reconstruir cadenas causales en la operatividad de estos sistemas hacen inviable el paradigma del control humano significativo, convirtiéndolo en una ficción normativa incapaz de asegurar una responsabilidad efectiva. A partir de este diagnóstico, se adopta un enfoque teórico-dogmático de orientación crítico-analítica para comprender la crisis de legitimidad provocada por la inteligencia artificial generativa. Los resultados muestran que la ausencia de sujetos humanos identificables vinculados causalmente a los efectos de estos modelos genera un vacío estructural de imputación, incompatible con las exigencias del Estado de Derecho. Se concluye que la creación de una personalidad jurídica algorítmica de carácter instrumental, inspirada en antecedentes como el peculium romano, constituye una alternativa normativamente coherente para restablecer centros funcionales de responsabilidad, garantizar la reparación y preservar la coherencia del sistema jurídico en contextos de agencia distribuida.

items.title: Different Logics, Similar Intentions: Heterogeneity in How Employees Evaluate AI Adoption
items.abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) adoption at work has documented heterogeneity in user attitudes and adoption profiles, but less is known about whether employees differ in how they weight adoption-relevant information. In a within-subject structured-profile experiment, 446 employees provided 7,136 intention judgments across 16 profiles that varied AI adoption benefits, barriers, replacement vulnerability, and anticipated work harm. Multilevel regression mixture model analysis identified four latent decision-policy classes with different estimated weights on opportunity and threat cues; class mean intentions were not statistically distinguishable. Drawing on multiple-cue judgment theory, we interpret this pattern as heterogeneity in cue utilization rather than simply in attitude levels. Explaining and managing AI adoption therefore requires attention to latent decision policies, because aggregate effect estimates and profiles based on mean levels can conceal differences in cue responsiveness that shape how employees evaluate AI.

items.title: EFFECT OF JOB ROTATION PROCEDURES ON EMPLOYEE ENGAGEMENT AT THE NATIONAL REGISTRATION BUREAU HEADQUARTERS IN NAIROBI CITY COUNTY, KENYA
items.abstract: Purpose of Study: This study examined the effect of job rotation procedures on employee engagement at the National Registration Bureau Headquarters in Nairobi City County, Kenya. Specifically, it assessed how job rotation contributes to employee skills development, motivation, teamwork and engagement. The study was guided by the Job Characteristics Model of work design. Methodology: The study adopted a descriptive research design targeting 154 employees through census sampling. Data were collected using structured questionnaires and semi-structured interviews. A total of 146 questionnaires were returned, representing a 94.8% response rate. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and regression analysis, alongside qualitative thematic analysis. Findings: The findings revealed positive perceptions of job rotation procedures, particularly skills development (M = 4.24), teamwork (M = 4.22), motivation (M = 4.21) and task exposure (M = 4.17). Employee engagement was high, with mean scores ranging from 4.21 to 4.23. Correlation analysis established a strong positive relationship between job rotation procedures and employee engagement (r = .741, p < .01). Regression analysis demonstrated a statistically significant positive effect (B = 0.312, β = .324, p < .001). These results indicate that structured job rotation procedures are associated with improved employee engagement, supporting the Job Characteristics Model. Conclusion: The study concluded that job rotation procedures significantly enhance employee engagement through skills development, motivation and collaboration. It recommends institutionalising competency-based rotation policies, providing appropriate training, ensuring transparent communication and regularly monitoring implementation. These measures can strengthen employee commitment, promote professional development and improve workforce effectiveness within public institutions.

items.title: Employment law, work engagement and AI governance: An integrative framework for AI-mediated employment in Europe
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into recruitment, performance evaluation, employee monitoring, and workplace decision-making raises important questions about employee rights, organizational accountability, and the conditions necessary for sustainable work engagement. Although existing research has examined the motivational consequences of AI-enabled work, the integration of employment law, AI governance, and established work-engagement principles remains insufficiently developed. This study develops an integrative analytical framework connecting five established work-engagement principles with AI governance and employment-law considerations in the European context. Drawing on an integrative literature review of motivational theories, contemporary research on AI-enabled work, responsible AI governance, and relevant European Union regulatory instruments, the study examines how five governance dimensions (lawful and proportionate AI use; equality and non-discrimination; employee voice and procedural rights; human oversight and accountability; and transparent evaluation and fair reward allocation) extend the application of these principles to AI-mediated employment. The framework draws on Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) theory to explain how AI-related organizational practices and legal-institutional governance may shape employee experiences and influence whether AI-mediated working conditions are perceived as job resources or job demands, with potential implications for work engagement. The study's originality lies in integrating established AI governance considerations with established work-engagement principles rather than proposing entirely new governance principles. It contributes an interdisciplinary theoretical perspective while recognizing the need for future empirical validation and jurisdiction-specific legal analysis. The framework may inform managerial and policy discussions on developing fair, accountable, and employee-centered AI-enabled workplaces across Europe.

items.title: Evaluating AI Alignment in LLMs: Output Analysis of Value Priorities Across 75 Models with Human Benchmarking
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) shape human–AI interaction, yet capability and safety benchmarks provide limited insight into their expressed value priorities. Across three studies, we developed an output-based approach to evaluating correspondence between LLM priorities and human judgements of optimal AI functioning. Study 1 identified six themes through inductive qualitative analysis: Performance, Adaptive Capacity, Social Good, Ethics and Responsibility, Relational Integration, and Agency. Study 2 found stable rankings within models and a shared priority structure across models. Study 3 compared 75 LLMs with 376 human respondents using a profile-fidelity metric combining profile shape and calibration of between-priority differences. Many models reproduced the human profile while exaggerating differences between priorities. Fidelity varied across models, with no clear pattern linking fidelity to more recent releases. Both humans and LLMs assigned Agency low priority. This framework offers a standardized method for auditing expressed value profiles across models alongside capability, safety, and output evaluations.

items.abstract: As digital assistants become increasingly integrated into safety-critical environments, explainable AI is expected to support operator understanding and decision-making. From a human-machine interface design perspective, how explanations are presented is an important consideration. This exploratory, design-focused study investigates the usefulness and user experience of storytelling video-based explanations compared with text-based explanations in a simulated emergency involving drone and Urban Air Mobility traffic management. Explanation content was structured using Construal Level Theory to provide incremental levels of detail. Nine licensed air traffic controllers participated in a mixed-methods, within-participants study, assuming the speculative role of UAM Coordinator responsible for low-altitude airspace safety. Eight of nine participants preferred the storytelling video format, describing it as more engaging and supportive of understanding and decision confidence. However, some perceived that the system had already made the decision, raising concerns about human agency. Video also offered limited flexibility for revisiting information, whereas text enabled self-paced reading and review but was perceived as more stressful to process. Rather than establishing the superiority of either format, the findings provide preliminary design insights into balancing engagement, user control, and human agency in explainable AI interfaces for future UAM operations.

items.title: Exploring the Day-To-Day Carryover of Change-Oriented Behavior in Organizations: The Role of Emotional Appraisal Competencies
items.abstract: Change-oriented behavior (CB), that is, self-directed actions that question and seek to improve how work gets done, is one way employees drive constructive change at work. Although CB is dynamic and primarily driven by affective processes, less is known about individual differences in day-to-day carryover (i.e. the extent to which yesterday’s change behavior predicts today’s) and about the role of inner personal resources, such as emotional appraisal. Integrating cognitive evaluation theory and conservation of resources theory, we examined whether self-emotional appraisal (SEA) and others’ emotional appraisal (OEA) relate to carryover patterns of CB. Employees from Greece (N = 602) completed a quantitative diary over five consecutive workdays. Results from multilevel autoregressive analysis revealed moderate, positive day-to-day CB carryover with significant between-person variation. Both mean levels of SEA and OEA predicted carryover strength, controlling for mean CB and trait affectivity. SEA showed comparable effects on baseline levels and carryover, whereas OEA showed much stronger effects on levels than carryover, suggesting functional differentiation. Baseline CB strongly negatively related to carryover, indicating that behavioral level and temporal carryover represent distinct constructs. The study contributes to both theory and practice by clarifying how distinct emotional competencies support the maintenance of change-directed effort over time.

items.title: Feeling Easier, Working Harder: Cognitive Load in AI-Assisted Code Comprehension
items.abstract: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. While these tools aim to reduce the difficulty of reading code, interacting with them introduces a dual-task environment that may impose extraneous cognitive load that is challenging to capture. This study investigates how access to generative AI affects developers' real-time cognitive workload, code comprehension performance, and self-perceived code comprehension strategies. We conducted a 3x2 within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students reviewing Java code snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Cognitive workload was continuously captured using a Detection-Response Task (tDRT) during both reading and quiz phases, and compared to post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

items.title: From Briefing to Prompt: How Users Translate Textual Design Instructions into Text-to-Image Prompts
items.abstract: Text-to-image systems support creative, educational, and professional work, yet how users translate briefs into effective prompts remains underexplored. This study examines prompt formulation and refinement by 23 participants using ChatGPT with DALL·E 3 under two task configurations: low-detail briefings with multiple reformulations and high-detail briefings with one reformulation. A structured literature review and qualitative analysis of 81 prompts, 81 images, interviews, and observation notes, supported by inter-coder agreement, identified recurring strategies, difficulties expressing visual intentions, and refinement patterns. High-detail/single-reformulation tasks produced semantically denser prompts and closer alignment with intended outcomes; low-detail/multiple-reformulation tasks encouraged exploratory prompting and interpretive variation. Because briefing detail and reformulation opportunities varied together, these findings reflect task-configuration differences, not isolated effects of briefing complexity. Framing prompting as cognitive and creative mediation in human–AI interaction, the study proposes a process model spanning briefing interpretation, semantic extraction, visual attribute selection, prompt structuring, generation, and refinement, requiring further validation.

items.title: From driving (L0) to living (L5): Intergenerational car comfort concept by Etic-emic theory
items.abstract: This study explores intergenerational vehicle comfort using the Etic-Emic framework, translating a psychological concept into automotive guidelines. A scoping review identified 34 parameters, and trend analysis of 1789 Scopus articles (1953-2025) tracing comfort across vehicle generations. Expert interviews with 15 specialists classified them as Etic (relevant to L0 and L5) or Emic (emerging specifically in L5), suggesting additional factors. Group brainstorming refined classifications, yielding 44 parameters, including factors such as brand identity and cargo space. Safety, vibration control, and fuel efficiency were stable Etic parameters, whereas non-driving tasks, confidence to sleep or fully recline, legal liability transparency, and cybersecurity were Emic. The novel "Intergenerational Car Comfort" concept provides OEMs an actionable decision tool: its Etic-Emic matrix guides trade-offs, including safety constraints versus expectations to recline and sleep. Ultimately, it identifies legacy architectures to retain or those requiring new interior packaging and HMI solutions, providing a roadmap for next-generation automated vehicles.

items.title: FROM GENERATIVE AI TO AGENTIC LEARNING SYSTEMS: A HUMANAI COLLABORATION FRAMEWORK FOR THE FUTURE OF DISTANCE HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: Generative AI entered universities as a tool that students consult on demand. The next generation of systems, AI agents that plan, remember and act over several steps, will take over parts of teaching, and distance education will feel this first. This article asks how responsibility should be divided between people and such agents in distance higher education. Following design science methodology, it combines an integrative review of experimental and survey evidence published in 2019-2026, regulatory documents and enrolment data for Uzbekistan. The evidence points in one direction: the same models raise or lower learning depending on how they are constrained. An AI tutor built around expert-written scaffolding produced learning gains 0.73 to 1.3 standard deviations larger than active learning in class, while unrestricted GPT-4 access raised practice scores by 48% but lowered later exam scores by 17%. Student use of AI is close to universal (92-95% in UK surveys, 60-72% in Uzbek samples), yet only about a third of students report receiving institutional training. In Uzbekistan, correspondence and distance students account for 32% of 1.85 million students, with 36 students per teacher. The proposed framework defines five levels of AI agency, from tool to orchestrating agent, and assigns each distance learning task a maximum level using three criteria: the stakes of the decision, the reversibility of errors and the strength of evidence. Tutoring and formative feedback may reach the tutor agent level under teacher oversight, whereas grading, progression and admission remain human decisions. Recommendations for universities and national AI policy follow.
